characters.name: Nahum

genealogy.note: The text gives no genealogy for Nahum, only his gentilic 'the Elkoshite' (Nahum 1:1), identifying him by hometown rather than lineage. Elkosh's location is not stated anywhere in this text and remains unidentified here.

verses.note: "The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite." The only verse naming him; everything else is his oracle, not narrated biography.

"Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee he is utterly cut off." Nahum's own herald-imagery for the announcement his prophecy brings to Judah.

funFacts: Nahum's name means 'comfort'/'consoler' - fitting, since his message comforts Judah by pronouncing the downfall of its oppressor Nineveh.
NAMING COLLISION: the underlying name 'Nahum' also appears (as 'Naum') in Jesus's genealogy in Luke - a different, unrelated individual; not merged here.
Nahum's entire book is one continuous oracle against a foreign nation with no call narrative and no oracle against Judah/Israel itself - unusual among the Minor Prophets.

characters.name: Nineveh (the Burden of Nineveh)
characters.purpose: The book's central oracle: a formal doom-pronouncement against Nineveh, declaring its total destruction as judgment for its cruelty - the city that had 'afflicted' Judah (1:12) and is called a 'bloody city... full of lies and robbery' (3:1) that sold nations through 'whoredoms' and 'witchcrafts' (3:4). Teaches that the LORD is 'slow to anger' yet will 'not at all acquit the wicked' (1:3).

verses.note: The oracle's formal heading: "The burden of Nineveh."
"But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies." Source of this tier's flood imagery.
"...I will cut off the graven image and the molten image: I will make thy grave for thou art vile." Addressed to the king/gods of Assyria.
The siege breaks: "the gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved... Nineveh is of old like a pool of water: yet they shall flee away."
Nineveh mocked as an emptied lions' den: "Where is the dwelling of the lions...? Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts."
"Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery... because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts."
"...Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?"
Closing dirge addressed to 'the king of Assyria' (unnamed): "thy nobles shall dwell in the dust... there is no healing of thy bruise."

funFacts: 'Burden' is the standard term elsewhere for a doom-oracle against a foreign nation - Nahum's whole book follows that same form, aimed entirely at Nineveh.

This translation, like KJV, capitalizes 'Huzzab' (2:7) as though a proper name ('Huzzab shall be led away captive') - deliberately not given its own character entry here since the underlying phrase is genuinely disputed (possibly a verb, not a name).

characters.name: No (No-amon / Thebes)
characters.purpose: A historical precedent cited within the oracle: the Egyptian city of No (Thebes) fell to conquest despite rivers, a sea-like rampart, and the combined strength of Ethiopia and Egypt defending it (3:8-9) - Nahum argues that if No could still fall, Nineveh's defenses will not save it either ('Art thou better than populous No...', 3:8).

verses.note: "Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?"
"Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite Put and Lubim were thy helpers."

"Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains."

funFacts: No-amon is the ancient Egyptian city Thebes ('city of Amon'), rendered here simply 'No,' matching the KJV form.
Ethiopia, Egypt, Put, and Lubim (3:9) are named as nations/allies supplying No's strength, not individuals - no personal character treatment given to them in this book.

status: drafted via lean single-pass workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text
notes: Read the full Ethiopian translation text (3 chapters, 15+13+19=47 verses) directly - content is textually identical in substance to the KJV Nahum already indexed (Assets/Resources/Bible/CharacterIndex/Nahum.json), with only minor archaic-phrasing/wording variance (e.g. 1:2 reads a doubled clause vs KJV's single clause; 1:15 has an extra phrase vs KJV). No new named individuals, no chapter/verse restructuring, no Ezra-style canonical divergence here - this book is a straightforward match, so the KJV's 3-tier structure (one person tier for the prophet, two law/theme tiers for the oracle-against-Nineveh and the No/Thebes historical precedent) was reused and re-verified line-by-line against this translation's own text rather than invented fresh. All ids suffixed _ethiopian to avoid cross-translation collision. NAMING COLLISION (carried over, re-verified against this translation - the name-collision concerns a different book, not this text): the underlying name "Nahum" appears elsewhere in Scripture as "Naum" (an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy) - unrelated to this prophet, flagged not merged. INTENTIONAL NON-ENTRY: "Huzzab" (2:7) is capitalized as a proper name in this translation just as in KJV, but the underlying phrase is genuinely disputed (may be a verb, "it is decreed," not a name) - deliberately not given a character entry, per the no-invention rule. No bulk genealogyLists needed - only two law-tiers, no genealogical lists in this book. Roster is intentionally thin (1 person-tier, 2 law-tiers) because Nahum is only 3 chapters and is a single continuous oracle against Nineveh with essentially no other named individuals - reflects real book content, not incomplete indexing.
